title: What Is an Agentic Enrichment Spreadsheet?
summary: An agentic enrichment spreadsheet is a sheet where each column is an AI agent that researches every row. How it differs from Clay and AI SDRs.
body_markdown:
> **Definition:** An agentic enrichment spreadsheet is a spreadsheet where each column is an AI agent. You describe what a column should find, and the agent researches every row using data providers and the web, citing sources and leaving cells empty when nothing verifies.


*Disclosure: Orange Slice, the publisher of this page, makes an agentic enrichment spreadsheet. We explain the category in general terms and say where other approaches fit better.*


## How an agentic enrichment spreadsheet works


A normal sales spreadsheet holds data someone typed or imported. An enrichment spreadsheet fills data in automatically. An *agentic* one goes further: each column has an instruction, and an AI agent carries it out row by row. The agent decides which provider to call, when to search the web, and what to do if a lookup fails.


Four ideas define the category:


1. **Columns are instructions, not formulas.** "Find the person this role reports to" is a column. So is "Does this company sell to hospitals? Yes/No, with a source."
2. **Columns depend on each other.** A buyer column needs the company domain first, and an email column needs the buyer. The sheet runs them in order.
3. **Waterfalls behind the scenes.** For a contact detail, the agent tries several providers in turn and stops when one returns a verified result.
4. **Empty beats wrong.** A good agentic sheet leaves a cell blank when there's no source, rather than guessing.


Orange Slice's[YC company page](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/orange-slice) describes its version as "a spreadsheet where every column is TypeScript—and AI writes it for you": you describe the column in chat, and it generates the code and runs it across thousands of rows.


## Example: columns as agents


Say you sell sales-coaching software to B2B SaaS companies that are building an outbound team. Here's the sheet as five column instructions:


Column The agent's instruction


Careers page Find the company's careers page or ATS job board


Trigger role From postings in the last 30 days, list any SDR, BDR or first AE roles


Pain line Quote one sentence from that posting that shows a sales problem


Buyer Name, title and LinkedIn URL of the person the role reports to


Verified email The buyer's work email, verified; empty if not found


And here's what the rows might look like. **Illustrative example data with made-up companies.**


Company (example) Trigger role Pain line Buyer Verified email


Example Ledger Co First Account Executive "Own the full cycle as our first AE" CEO found


Sample Ops Inc 2× SDR "Help us build outbound from scratch" Head of Sales found


Demo Analytics none — — —


Notice the third row: no trigger, so the downstream columns stay empty. Nothing is invented. For the full version of this recipe, see[how to find high-intent B2B prospects from job postings](https://www.orangeslice.ai/blog/find-high-intent-b2b-prospects-job-postings) .


## Agentic spreadsheet vs Clay tables vs AI SDRs


These three get mixed up, but they do different jobs.


Agentic enrichment spreadsheet Clay-style table AI SDR


**What you do** Describe the list or column in plain language Build the table column by column, choosing providers Set goals and messaging; the tool prospects and sends


**Output** A sheet of researched rows you review A sheet of enriched rows you review Sent emails and booked meetings


**Human control** High: you see every cell and source before outreach High: you design every step Lower: the tool acts on your behalf


**Learning curve** Low to start Higher; very flexible once learned Low to start, harder to tune


**Best for** Signal-based lists, research-heavy targeting Complex, custom workflows at scale High-volume top-of-funnel


**Clay tables** are the closest relative. Clay includes AI agents ("Claygents") inside its tables and a marketplace of 150+ providers ([clay.com/pricing](https://www.clay.com/pricing) ). The difference is mostly where you start: in Clay you design the table; in an agentic spreadsheet you describe the outcome and the agent designs the table. We go deeper in[Orange Slice vs Clay](https://www.orangeslice.ai/compare/clay) .


**AI SDRs** automate sending as well as research. That's useful for volume, but you give up review of each row before it goes out. Many teams pair a research sheet with a sequencer they control. For a database-plus-sequencing approach, see[Orange Slice vs Apollo](https://www.orangeslice.ai/compare/apollo) , or the three-way[Clay vs Apollo vs Orange Slice](https://www.orangeslice.ai/blog/clay-vs-apollo-vs-orange-slice) comparison.
